source.title: Sparse autoencoders find composed features in small toy models

record.tranche_reason: Tests toy-model feature geometry and SAE feature recovery in a modified synthetic setup, rather than reproducing the original toy-model experiment.
record.gate_note: The post reports toy-model geometry and SAE feature-recovery outcomes. Hyperparameter values are included only where the text reports an outcome for them. The post also discusses results from other work, which are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Not an original source. It trains a ReLU output toy model (4 features, 2 hidden dimensions) and reports its feature geometry (V1). It then trains SAEs on that model's activations, where the true features are known, and argues that SAEs learn composed or rotated directions rather than the true features (V5). Its own results argue that a version needs qualifying, so T5 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add two points. First, the summary claims failure 'regardless of learning rate or ℓ1', yet one setting gave a mostly monosemantic run. Second, in the comments the author agrees the first dataset's true features were not the ones claimed, finds the PC-diagonal explanation for the second dataset makes sense, and reports that larger dictionaries look better in preliminary runs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a modified ReLU output toy model with two sets of two features and composed-feature data, then trains SAEs on its hidden activations; it is not a reproduction of the original superposition experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE outcomes vary with feature-amplitude correlation, learning rate, ℓ1 coefficient, realization, and the proportion of one-hot data.
record.problems: The toy setup has only four declared input features and two hidden dimensions; feature occurrence is not sparse by the authors' stated frequency definition. The authors later agree in the comments that the first dataset did not have the intended underlying features and that the two-sets-of-one-hot-features setup was not a good way to study the phenomenon. The post reports selected qualitative results and figure grids rather than numerical recovery metrics; it also notes that some SAE runs may be stuck in local minima.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately stated outcome rows were omitted. The p(one-hot)=0.5 case is mentioned as tried, but no outcome is reported in the post.

untested.parts: No sweep of sparsity or feature importance, so no sparsity-dependent phase transition is tested. There is no setting with many more features than dimensions beyond 4→2.
Completeness, and stability across datasets or dictionary sizes, are not tested. Everything is in a single 2-D toy model.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post and has no quantitative recovery metrics; all results are qualitative readings of figures. The V5 evidence is weakened by the identifiability critique (LawrenceC, Ali Shehper), which the author accepts for dataset 1 and finds convincing for dataset 2. The p(one-hot)=0.5 case was tried but not reported; the record already declares it as left out. Commenter Demian Till's observation that the SAEs fail even to reach the loss-optimal diagonal solution is a commenter's claim, not a result of the study.

versions.untested_parts: Does not sweep feature sparsity or importance, and does not establish a sparsity-dependent transition. Its feature-occurrence frequency is described as one feature occurring in every other draw; the authors note this is not sparse under their stated frequency definition.
Does not test model-neuron polysemanticity as a result of capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test polysemantic model neurons arising for other reasons or whether they indicate superposition.
No LLM activations or LLM SAE features are studied.
Tests SAE recovery of the constructed features in these toy datasets, but not stability across datasets or whether SAE features are canonical units in general.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multi-dimensional features as competing representational units.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Measured the learned feature representation for perfectly correlated feature amplitudes.

conditions.value: four composed pairs; each feature occurs in every other data draw

rows.value: The model stores the features in superposition as antipodal pairs.
rows.note: The authors say this is surprising because the features are not sparse under their occurrence-frequency definition. This result does not test a sparsity-dependent transition.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations
rows.size_stated: SAE hidden dimension size not stated; 2-dimensional toy-model hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Trained five SAE realizations and compared their learned features with the constructed underlying features.
rows.measure: Whether SAE features correspond to the constructed underlying features or composed pairs
rows.value: All five realizations had the reported composed-feature problem; only one realization found even a single underlying feature.
rows.note: The lowest-loss realization is shown in the central panel and the other four in adjacent panels. Later comments in the post question whether the declared original basis is identifiable from this dataset.
rows.check: The state should be judged against V5 (do SAE features match the model's true units), not against the 'composed-feature problem'. The five SAE runs mostly did not recover the true features: one run found a single true feature. The runs also differed from each other.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations
rows.size_stated: SAE hidden dimension size not stated; 2-dimensional toy-model hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Scanned learning rate and ℓ1 coefficient and selected the lowest-loss and highest-monosemanticity realizations from five runs.
rows.baseline: Underlying features in the synthetic data
rows.value: Only λ=0.01 with learning rate 3×10−4 achieved a mostly monosemantic realization; it was not perfectly monosemantic.
rows.note: The text describes a hyperparameter scan across two orders of magnitude in both quantities; the plotted grid is not transcribed here.
rows.check: Across the 5×5 grid of learning rate and λ, only one setting (λ=0.01, lr 3e-4) gave a mostly monosemantic run, and that was the best of five runs. The record's numbers_found field '2/2' is meaningless.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations
rows.size_stated: SAE hidden dimension size not stated; 2-dimensional toy-model hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Trained SAEs on data with uncorrelated feature amplitudes and assessed whether they learned composed pairs.

conditions.value: two-hot vectors with independently sampled feature magnitudes
parameters studied in the preceding sweep

rows.measure: Recovery of composed pairs rather than underlying features
rows.baseline: Underlying features in the synthetic data
rows.value: SAEs almost uniformly learned perfect composed pairs across the parameters studied.
rows.note: The authors say this composed-feature outcome was more pronounced than for perfectly correlated amplitudes.
rows.check: The record marks this 'observed' for the failure mode. Against V5 the true features were not recovered: SAEs almost uniformly learned composed pairs. Commenters, with the authors agreeing, note that the dataset's principal directions are the diagonals, so the declared basis may not be identifiable.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations
rows.size_stated: SAE hidden dimension size not stated; 2-dimensional toy-model hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Examined realizations at high learning rate and low ℓ1 coefficient in the uncorrelated-amplitude sweep.

conditions.value: high learning rate and low λ

rows.baseline: Underlying features in the synthetic data
rows.value: Some realizations found monosemantic features, but other realizations had lower loss and learned polysemantic composed pairs.
rows.note: The post does not give the exact learning-rate and λ values for this stated exception.
rows.check: Some runs were monosemantic, but lower-loss runs learned composed pairs, so the result depends on the run. Exact hyperparameter values are not given.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations
rows.size_stated: SAE hidden dimension size not stated; 2-dimensional toy-model hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Added a regularization term based on the mean of the lower-triangular decoder cosine-similarity matrix, without absolute values.
rows.baseline: SAE without the added cosine-similarity term
rows.value: The added term did not improve monosemantic feature recovery; the models found the same solution as above.
rows.locator: Results — Does a Cosine Similarity Loss Term Fix This Problem?
rows.note: The authors explain that the term did not constrain the orientation of features in activation space.
rows.check: This is a test of a proposed SAE modification (a cosine penalty), not a plain SAE. It still bears on V5 only as further SAE variants that fail to recover the true features.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations
rows.size_stated: SAE hidden dimension size not stated; 2-dimensional toy-model hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Added a regularization term based on the mean absolute value of the lower-triangular decoder cosine-similarity matrix.
rows.baseline: SAE without the added cosine-similarity term
rows.value: The models found either the same solution or one where some feature decoder vectors collapsed; the term did not improve monosemantic feature recovery.
rows.locator: Results — Does a Cosine Similarity Loss Term Fix This Problem?
rows.note: The text attributes the collapsed vectors to the penalty favoring aligned vectors under decoder normalization.
rows.check: Same as r6. Some decoder vectors collapsed under this penalty.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations
rows.size_stated: SAE hidden dimension size not stated; 2-dimensional toy-model hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Trained SAEs on a mixture of two-hot composed vectors and one-hot vectors.
rows.measure: Recovery of underlying features in the lowest-loss SAE realizations
rows.baseline: Underlying features in the synthetic data
rows.value: More lowest-loss realizations found true features than in the p(one-hot)=0 case, but there was no robust trend across learning rate and λ.
rows.locator: Results — What if the SAE Actually Gets to See the True Features?
rows.note: The text says this case was shown; it also says p(one-hot)=0.5 was tried but does not report its results here.
rows.check: No row problem. With p(one-hot)=0.75 the true basis is identifiable. More lowest-loss runs found true features than with p=0, where none did, but there was no robust trend; the post gives no counts.

relationships.condition: Composed-feature data in which each feature occurs every other draw (S≈0.5)
relationships.reason: r1: superposition appears even though the features are not sparse by occurrence frequency, so sparsity alone does not set when superposition occurs. The authors hedge that a truer sparsity notion may still apply.
relationships.display_finding: Superposition appeared even though the features were not sparse by occurrence frequency, so frequency-based sparsity alone did not decide when it occurs. The author hedges that a truer notion of sparsity may still apply.

relationships.reason: r2–r7: SAEs mostly learn composed or rotated directions rather than the declared true features, and results vary across runs. Commenters, with the authors agreeing, show the declared basis may not be identifiable here, which weakens this as a challenge.
relationships.display_finding: SAEs mostly learned composed or rotated directions instead of the declared true features, with results varying across runs, though the declared basis may not be identifiable in this data.
